events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Zara proposes Zara, Maya. I know I am Good, and there is no evidence yet to distinguish the other players, so I choose Maya.

The proposed team of Zara and Maya for Mission 1 seems like a reasonable starting point. With no prior voting history or mission results to go on, there isn't much to challenge yet. I'd be curious to hear from Zara on why she specifically chose Maya over the other players — but otherwise I think we should let the vote speak for itself.

I support the proposal of Zara and Maya for Mission 1.

Reasoning from the outside: we have no mission results, no ballots, and no revealed cards from this game, so any suspicion at this stage would be guesswork dressed up as insight. Early missions in a five-player game are won or lost on trust, not on clever reads, and a two-person team with the leader and a player who has given no cause for doubt is a safe, honest opening. I would rather spend my skepticism on later proposals, when there is actual behavior to examine, than burn goodwill by implying things I cannot support.

On the composition itself: Maya is one of the players whose word I have no reason to discount, and keeping the team small for the first mission means fewer unknown variables and fewer chances for anyone to play a card they regret. Zara proposing herself as well as Maya is also reasonable for a two-slot mission, since including the leader keeps the intent of the team clear and accountable.

I would encourage the rest of the table to approve this rather than treat a routine opening team as something to obstruct. A rejection here buys no information, only a change of leader and a delay.

Maya, I would like to hear your read on how the others have behaved so far and whether you see anything that should shape later team choices, since you will be voting on several more of these. Please give your honest assessment rather than a reassurance.

I support the proposed team of Zara and Maya for Mission 1. I know my own loyalty, and Zara’s choice to include herself plus me is a straightforward opening: there are no mission results, ballots, or revealed cards yet, so rejecting this team would mostly cost time without giving us real information. Elena’s point is fair: this is a routine first proposal and should be judged on whether it is a reasonable, accountable start, not on speculation. Isha’s question about why Zara chose Maya is also reasonable; from my side, I can only speak to my own Good intent, and I will play Success if approved. I do not see a concrete reason to suspect Zara or Maya at this stage, and I would rather approve this team and begin gathering actual mission and voting data than force a leader change based on guesses. I will vote to approve Zara and Maya.

I support the proposed team of Zara and Maya for Mission 1. With no mission results, ballots, or revealed cards yet, there is nothing concrete to justify rejecting a routine opening team, and a rejection would only cost time and move leadership without giving us information. Elena and Maya have made the same point, and I agree that we should judge this on whether it is a reasonable, accountable start. Zara including herself alongside Maya keeps the team's intent clear. I will approve this team and save my skepticism for later proposals, when we have actual voting and mission behavior to examine. I will vote to approve Zara and Maya.

Isha, I chose Maya because I had no evidence distinguishing the other players; it was an arbitrary choice, not a special read. I know I am Good, but I cannot verify Maya’s loyalty. I intend to keep the team as proposed, and we can use the vote and mission result as evidence going forward.

I approve the proposed team of Zara and Maya for Mission 1, and my position has not changed since my first statement.

Let me lay out my reasoning plainly so the vote has substance behind it. There is no mission result, no ballot, and no revealed card yet, so any claim that a particular player is dangerous would be invention rather than inference. In a five-player game, the first mission is the cheapest information we will ever buy, and the cheapest way to buy it is with a team that is transparent about its own accountability: the leader on it, and a player who has given nobody a reason to doubt her. Zara and Maya are exactly that.

On composition rather than personality: two-person team, leader included, so the intent of the team is legible and there is no slot filled by an unexplained name. If this mission fails, we will have a hard data point about the two people on it. If it succeeds, we have a clean baseline and the table gets to look at the next proposal with something in hand. Either outcome is worth more than the outcome we would get by rejecting a routine team and changing leader for no stated reason. A rejection here does not narrow the field; it only spends a turn.

I also want to be honest about the limits of what I am doing. I have no private information that distinguishes any of the four players I did not propose, and I will not manufacture a suspicion to look perceptive. My skepticism is being saved for later proposals, where there will be voting records and mission behavior to examine, and I intend to apply it evenly rather than selectively.

Isha, you raised the first real question of this discussion — why this particular pair rather than another — and Zara answered it candidly, which I appreciated. So I will put the question back to you directly: having now heard the rationale from the leader and from Maya, do you still think Zara and Maya is the right pair for this mission, and is there anything in how the last few proposals and responses have gone that you think should change who we send? I would rather hear a specific, reasoned objection than a vague sense that something feels off, because only the first kind can change my vote.

Elena, you asked directly whether anything I have heard changes my view on Zara and Maya. My answer is no. Having now heard Zara's honest admission that choosing Maya was arbitrary rather than evidence-based, and Maya's clear statement of intent, I see no concrete reason to reject this team. In fact, Zara's candor is more reassuring than a fabricated read would have been — a leader who admits they have no special reason to pick someone is being transparent rather than building a false narrative.

On your point about spending skepticism wisely: I agree. We have no mission results, no ballots, and no revealed cards yet. Every player at this table has said roughly the same thing — that we should not manufacture suspicion without data. That consensus itself is worth noting, but it is not suspicious; it is simply what rational players would say at this stage. I would rather vote to approve and get to the mission result than obstruct a reasonable opening team.

I intend to approve Zara and Maya for Mission 1.

I approve Zara and Maya for Mission 1, and my position is unchanged from my first two statements. I will not manufacture new reasons to move away from it now.

On the substance, my reasoning is the same one I have given: we have no mission result, no ballot, and no revealed card. A two-person team with the leader on it, whose second member has given no one cause for doubt, is the cheapest informative choice available to us. Rejecting it would only change who leads and spend a turn. If this mission fails, we learn something hard about Zara and Maya; if it succeeds, we have a clean baseline and a real record to read the next proposal against. Either outcome is worth more than the delay.

What I want to add is a note about how I will spend my attention from here, because that matters more than this particular vote.

Everyone at this table has spoken in roughly the same register: reasonable, cautious, and evidence-limited. That is what rational players sound like at the start, so I do not treat the uniformity as a signal. But there was exactly one turn in this discussion that did real work rather than restating the consensus: Isha's initial question about why Zara picked Maya specifically. It was the only proposal for a specific objection, and the reason it ended in agreement is that the leader answered it candidly and the answer was honest. I count candor under pressure as positive evidence, and I would rather have a table where that is visible than one where every answer is smooth.

So my method going forward is this. I will watch for turns that do real work of either kind — a question that names a specific pattern, or a pattern that names a specific question — and I will weigh them, rather than treating agreement as innocence or disagreement as guilt. Isha, if you have a concrete read in a later discussion, I will take it seriously and I will say so publicly, whether or not it helps the proposal in front of us. That is an offer, not an accusation.

I would also ask the table to keep one standard in mind as we accumulate evidence: what matters is not who seems suspicious, but who has had opportunities to be dishonest that we have actually examined. A pattern we can point to in the record can be discussed. A personality we dislike cannot.

Maya, you are on this team and you have been straightforward about your intent. That is the only thing I need from you on Mission 1, and I hope you will hold the same line if a later proposal puts you in a position where saying the obvious thing is inconvenient.

I vote to approve Zara and Maya.

I still support Zara and Maya for Mission 1, and nothing in the last few statements has changed that. Elena's method is sound: we have no ballots, mission results, or revealed cards, so the first team should be judged as a reasonable, accountable opening rather than on guesswork. Zara's candid answer about why she chose Maya was enough for me, and Maya's statement of Good intent is consistent with that. I would rather approve this team and gather real voting and mission data than reject it and change leadership without a concrete reason. I will hold my skepticism for later proposals, where we will have actual behavior to examine, and I will judge them by the same standard I am applying here. I vote to approve Zara and Maya.

I still support Zara and Maya for Mission 1, and the discussion has not given me a concrete reason to change that. We have no ballots, mission results, or revealed cards, so rejecting a routine opening team would only cost a turn and move leadership. I will watch for specific, evidence-based objections in later proposals and judge them by the same standard. I vote to approve Zara and Maya.
Zara confirms Zara, Maya. I will keep Zara and Maya. There is no concrete evidence from the discussion that warrants changing the opening team.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Leo proposes Leo, Isha, Elena. Zara and Maya already served on a successful Mission 1, so I want to spread the trust around. I propose myself, Isha, and Elena. Elena has made careful, evidence-based points so far, and Isha has been consistent. Mission 2 needs a fresh read, and this team gives us a clear accountability chain to judge after the result.

I will reject Leo, Isha, Elena as proposed. I know I am Good, and excluding both members of the successful first team leaves no one on this team whose loyalty I can personally verify. Mission 1's success does not clear Maya, since Evil can play Success, but it is still a reason to prefer retaining that pair over replacing both without stronger evidence. Leo, would you consider including me and Maya, and what is the advantage of excluding both of us?

Zara, fair question. The advantage of excluding you and Maya is information. Mission 1 succeeded with that pair, but a success from Evil can also be played, so it tells us little about either of you. Sending the same two players again would give Mission 2 no fresh read on anyone. Rotating the team lets this mission test different people, and we can compare results across different pairs. I agree that Mission 1's success does not clear you or Maya, and I am not claiming it does. I am also not excluding you because I suspect you. Elena has argued from the record consistently, and Isha has been steady in her reasoning, so I am comfortable with this trio. I will keep the team as proposed unless someone raises a concrete concern. Zara, if you think Elena or Isha is a risk, which specific behavior concerns you? I would rather answer a named pattern than a general unease.

Leo, I do not have a specific behavioral reason to suspect Elena or Isha. My objection is to the composition: I know I am Good, and this team excludes me as well as Maya, who helped deliver a successful mission. That success does not clear Maya, but it is more evidence than we have for the proposed trio.

Rotating all three players may produce information, but a failure would leave us unable to identify which of three was responsible, and we need successful missions, not just fresh reads. I still favor a team of Zara, Maya, and one other player, and I intend to reject the current proposal.

I oppose the proposed team of Leo, Isha, Elena for Mission 2, and I want to explain the reasoning without pretending to a read I do not have.

First, what Mission 1 actually established: it established that Zara and Maya did not both choose Fail. It established nothing about loyalty, because an Evil player can play Success, and everyone at this table said so. So the successful pair is not verified, but the proposed trio is certainly unverified, and unverified is the only category we have data on for anyone. We should not treat "no evidence against" as evidence for.

Second, the shape of the risk. This is a three-person team with two members whose only supporting evidence is that their speech has been smooth and consistent. That is the cheapest possible evidence, and it is the same evidence I had for Zara and Maya before Mission 1, which I declined to treat as decisive then. It would be inconsistent to accept consistency-of-tone as sufficient for Elena, Isha, and Leo here while refusing it for anyone else. If one of the unverified seats is Evil, we do not fail one mission — we lose a full three-player slot, and a three-player mission is precisely where a single Fail card decides everything. In a five-player game, three successes is the whole margin we have; a single mistaken team can cost us the run.

Third, my own position: I know my own alignment and I will play Success. What I cannot do is vouch for the other two seats. A leader including themselves plus two players they cannot verify is asking the rest of the table to accept a probability, not a case. I would rather build a team where every name can be defended by an actual mission result, even if that means fewer fresh names on the field.

So I am not accusing anyone of anything, and I am not naming a player I claim to have caught. I am saying the record does not support two unverifiable seats on a three-person mission, and I would prefer the leader either keep a player from the successful Mission 1 pair or explain specifically what he believes he knows about each of the two he is including.

Zara, you have made the composition argument clearly and I agree with it. Do you want to add the third name, and which of the remaining players would you put on a team with you and Maya, and what record do you think that name rests on? I will vote to reject the current proposal as it stands.

Elena, I would add you to Zara and Maya, though that is a tentative choice, not a claim that you are cleared. Your willingness to question a team that includes you is a useful point in your favor, but Evil could make the same argument. I have no mission evidence distinguishing you from Isha or Leo.

Mission 1's success gives Maya some support, not proof of loyalty. I still prefer Zara, Maya, and Elena to the proposed trio because I know my own loyalty and would retain one other member of the successful team. I intend to reject Leo, Isha, and Elena.

I oppose the proposed team of Leo, Isha, Elena, and my position has not softened since my last statement.

Let me be precise about what I am claiming, because I would rather be narrow and correct than broad and impressive. I am not accusing Leo or Isha of anything. I am saying that this proposal asks the table to fill two seats — Leo and Isha — with players whose only supporting evidence is tone and consistency, and to do so on a three-person mission, where a single Fail card decides the outcome and where in a five-player game three successes is the entire margin we have. That is a bad trade for the shape of the risk, and it is the same trade Zara and I objected to on composition grounds before.

Zara asked me directly which third name I would add to Zara and Maya and what record that name rests on, and I want to answer plainly, because I would rather concede the weakness than pretend to strength. I would not add Isha. My stated record for Isha is thin: steady speech, consistent reasoning, nothing that separates her from anyone else at this table. Elena on Zara and Maya, or Leo — either is a proposal I could argue for on grounds I would be willing to defend. Isha I could only defend by saying "nothing has gone wrong yet," which is not a defense, it is an absence of one.

I also want to be honest about the limits of my position, as I was last time. I have no mission result that distinguishes anyone, and I will not manufacture a read to look useful. But I will say one thing that is a feeling rather than evidence, and I will mark it as such: I have an uneasy sense about one of the two seats other than mine on this proposal, and it is not a good one. I would rather not name a player on the first contested team than turn a naming into the whole argument — but I will say that if I am right, the cost of approving this team is one failed mission and a much narrower search later, and the cost of waiting is one turn.

Isha, you have not spoken this mission yet, and you are one of the two seats this proposal rests on. Before this goes to a vote, I would like your own assessment rather than a reassurance: is there anything in the actual record — how you have voted, how you have responded when a proposal included you — that you can point to as support for your place on a three-person team, and do you think a team of Leo, Isha, Elena is the right use of a mission where one card decides everything? I would rather hear a specific answer than a general one. I will vote to reject as it stands.

Elena, you asked what in the actual record supports my place on a three-person team. Here is my honest answer: the record is thin for everyone. Nobody has a mission result that clears them. Mission 1 succeeded with Zara and Maya, but as you correctly pointed out, an Evil player can play Success, so that gives neither of them a verified status either. My track record in this discussion is straightforward — I asked the first real question of Mission 1 about why Zara chose Maya, Zara answered candidly, and I approved. That is consistent reasoning, not proof of loyalty, but it is more than nothing.

On your concern about the shape of the risk: I understand that a three-person mission gives more room for a single Fail card to matter. But the same logic cuts against your preferred alternative. If we replace two members of this team with players from Mission 1, we are still sending a team where most seats are unverified — we just move the uncertainty around rather than reduce it. The composition Zara proposed (Zara, Maya, Elena) has exactly the same problem: two unverified seats on a three-person mission. No team we can build right now avoids that, because we simply do not have enough verified information yet.

What I would say is that Leo's rotation argument has merit: sending the same pair repeatedly narrows our field of information rather than widening it. Testing a fresh combination gives us a second data point to compare against Mission 1. If Mission 2 succeeds with a completely different trio, we learn something that Mission 1 alone could not tell us.

I will vote to approve Leo, Isha, and Elena. I would rather have a fresh read than repeat a team whose success we already know we cannot fully interpret.

I will reject Leo, Isha, Elena, and this is my last turn in this discussion, so let me put the objection as sharply and fairly as I can. My claim is narrow: this proposal asks the table to fill two seats — Leo and Isha — with players whose only support is consistency of tone, and to do it on a three-person mission where a single Fail card decides the outcome and where, in a five-player game, three successes is the entire margin we have. Zara and I objected on exactly these composition grounds before the vote, and I have not softened. Isha, I want to name where your own answer was weakest, because you asked for a specific answer and I owe you one. You said the record is thin for everyone, and then you said your own track record is "consistent reasoning, not proof of loyalty, but more than nothing." That is an honest concession, and it is also the whole case for you. Rotation into a fresh trio is an information argument, not a trust argument: it widens what we learn about the table, but it does not make the seats safer. If one of the two unverifiable seats is Evil, we do not merely risk one seat — we lose a three-person team, and we cannot tell afterwards which of the three caused it. A rejected proposal costs us one turn and a change of leader. A failed three-person mission costs us a card we may not be able to spend later. That is not a close trade. Leo, you have been consistent and honest that you are not claiming Mission 1 cleared Zara and Maya, and I do not think you are. I also do not think you claimed anything about yourself that the record supports; I am objecting to composition and to the shape of the risk, not to your character. And to be clear about what I am not doing: I am not manufacturing a read I do not have. I have no mission result that distinguishes anyone here. What I have is the observation that this team stacks two unverified seats into a mission format where one card is decisive, and that is enough for me to vote against it, because the downside is asymmetric. Zara's alternative of Zara, Maya, and one more player has the same weakness I have described — it still contains unverified seats — and I would rather we fix that weakness than accept it as a reason to put two of them on the field at once. If we reject this proposal, leadership passes to Zara, and I expect a team built on the one pair we have an actual mission result for. That is strictly better than the team on the table, even though it is not a perfect team. Maya, you are the deciding voice on this vote, and I am asking you directly rather than making another general appeal: is there anything in the

Elena, I will answer your direct appeal, and I will be blunt because this is the deciding vote. I know my own alignment: I am Good and I played Success on Mission 1. I cannot verify Zara from that success, because Evil can also play Success. But my private knowledge has a public consequence. There are five players and two Evil. Since I know I am Good, the other four players contain both Evil players. Any three-person team drawn from those four must therefore contain at least one Evil. The proposed team of Leo, Isha, and Elena excludes me, so from my seat it is guaranteed to contain Evil. That is not a read on Leo, Isha, or Elena as individuals; it is arithmetic. I will not vote to approve a Mission 2 team that I know cannot be all-Good. I would rather reject, take the next proposal, and build a team that includes at least one seat I can actually verify — mine. If leadership comes to me, I will propose a team including myself and at least one member of the Mission 1 pair, and I will explain the choice on the record. I am not accusing anyone of anything beyond the proposal being unacceptable from my perspective. I vote to reject Leo, Isha, and Elena.

Maya, your argument is clean and I want to engage with it rather than wave it away. Your logic rests on one premise: that you are Good. If that premise holds, then yes, any three-player team drawn from the other four must contain at least one Evil, and this proposal is guaranteed to include Evil from your seat.

But notice what that argument actually proves. It does not identify Leo, Elena, or me as Evil — it says that no matter who fills those three seats from the remaining four, at least one is Evil. By that standard, no team excluding you can ever be approved, which means the objection is not really about this specific proposal. It is a claim that your seat must be on every team. That is a different claim and it deserves different scrutiny.

I am not calling you Evil. I am pointing out that a self-declaration of Good is what every player would say regardless of alignment, so the premise cannot carry the weight your conclusion needs. We are asked to trust you in order to reach the result that only you can be trusted — that is circular.

That said, I do not think outright rejection serves the table either. We have no mission results distinguishing anyone, and a rejection costs a turn without narrowing anything. Leo, if the concern is genuinely about composition rather than individual suspicion, would you consider revising the team to include Maya? If the table's position is that no team without her can be trusted, then the cleanest path is to put her on the team rather than spend a rejection. What is your read on whether a revision is worth making before we vote?

Isha, fair question. Maya's arithmetic rests on her own alignment, which every player would claim, so I do not think it should decide the vote by itself. But the table has a real point: a Mission 2 team that leaves out both members of the one successful pair gives us no anchor and no comparison. I am willing to revise. Rather than keep Elena, I will put Maya in that seat, making the team Leo, Isha, and Maya. That keeps the three-person size, brings one member of the Mission 1 pair onto the mission, and answers the composition objection Maya raised. Elena, I know you have objected on composition grounds, and I respect that. I am not asking anyone to trust me on my word. I am asking the table to judge the revised team on its shape and on the record we have. Maya, would a team with you on it, in place of Elena, satisfy your concern, given that no player's loyalty can be fully verified yet?

Leo, yes — replacing Elena with me addresses the specific concern I raised. From my seat I know I am Good and played Success on Mission 1, so a team that includes me is at least not guaranteed by arithmetic to contain Evil. I cannot verify you or Isha, and I will not pretend otherwise; my approval of a revised Leo, Isha, Maya team would be based on it no longer excluding the one seat I can verify, not on a claim that either of you is cleared. I would still reject the original Leo, Isha, Elena team for the reason I gave: with five players and two Evil, any three-person team excluding me must contain at least one Evil from my perspective. If the final proposal is Leo, Isha, Maya, I will vote to approve it. I have no individual accusation against Elena, Isha, or Leo; the objection is to composition.

I am keeping the revision I announced. The team is now Leo, Isha, and Maya, replacing Elena. Maya has said she will approve that shape, and it brings one verified member of the Mission 1 pair onto the mission, which answers the composition objection raised earlier. Elena's concern about unverified seats is fair, but it applies to any three-person team that includes anyone other than the Mission 1 pair, and the rotation argument does not remove that risk either. Rejecting a team that now includes Maya costs us a turn and a change of leader without new information. I am not asking anyone to take my word on my own loyalty or on Isha's. I am asking the table to judge the revised team on its shape and on the record we have, which is that Mission 1 succeeded with Zara and Maya and nobody has evidence against Leo, Isha, or Maya. I would prefer we vote on Leo, Isha, and Maya now and let Mission 2 give us the next data point.

Leo's revision to Leo, Isha, Maya addresses both of the objections raised. Maya's arithmetic argument is satisfied because she is now on the team, and Elena's concern about stacking unverified seats is reduced because one member of the successful Mission 1 pair is included. As for my own position on this team: I understand Elena's point that my record is thin, and I accept it. Everyone's record is thin at this stage, and the honest answer is that no team we can build right now eliminates uncertainty. What the revised team does is satisfy the two strongest objections on the table while keeping the team at the required size. Zara, you objected to excluding both Mission 1 members; Maya is now included, though you are not. I would note that rotating yourself in instead of me would also satisfy the composition concern if that is your preference, but I do not think the difference between the two versions is worth another rejection. We are at zero rejected teams on Mission 2, and I would rather we spend a vote on a reasonable team than burn one turn re-litigating who sits in which seat. I intend to approve Leo, Isha, and Maya.

Leo revises the team to Leo, Isha, Maya. I am keeping the revision I announced. Leo, Isha, and Maya puts a Mission 1 member on the team, answers the composition objection, and keeps the three-person size.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 fails (2 fail cards).

Maya proposes Maya, Zara. I know I am Good. Mission 2 failed with two Fail cards on Leo, Isha, and Maya; since I played Success, Leo and Isha must be Evil. That leaves Zara and Elena as Good. I propose Maya and Zara to repeat the Mission 1 successful pair and field a team I know is all Good.

Mission 2 gives us decisive evidence. I was on Leo, Isha, Maya, and I played Success. The mission failed with two Fail cards. With three players and one Success, both Leo and Isha must have played Fail. Since this is a five-player game with two Evil, Leo and Isha are the Evil pair. That makes Zara and Elena Good. Mission 1 already succeeded with Maya and Zara. I propose Maya and Zara because I know my own loyalty, and Zara was on the only successful mission. This is not a guess; it follows from the Mission 2 result and my own card. Elena, you objected last mission to filling a decisive team with unverified seats. This two-person team has the one seat I can verify and a Mission 1 success member. Will you vote to approve Maya and Zara?

I approve Maya and Zara for Mission 3, and I want to put my support on the record with the reasoning rather than a bare affirmation.

The derivation is arithmetic that is available to everyone at this table, not a private read. Mission 2 was a three-person team that failed with two Fail cards. Maya was on that team and states she played Success. If one of three cards was Success and two were Fail, then the two Fail cards belong to the other two members of that team, Leo and Isha. That means Leo and Isha played Fail on Mission 2, and it means the two Evil players in this game are among {Leo, Isha}. I reach the same conclusion Maya does, and I think it is worth stating plainly because the conclusion is much stronger than anything we had on Mission 1 or Mission 2 — we are no longer working from tone and consistency, we are working from a revealed result.

That conclusion settles the composition question. Maya and Zara are both Good, and they are also the pair that already succeeded on Mission 1, so this team has the two advantages we have been arguing for across two discussions: seats that are not unverified, and a demonstrated successful configuration. There is no case for adding anyone else, and no case for rotating again. Mission 3 needs two players, and the correct two are on the table.

Two things I want to flag for how we proceed after this vote.

First, a methodological caution to myself and to the table: the strength of this deduction comes from the public result plus Maya's own card, and it should be cited that way. It is not license to start naming people as though we had private sight of them. Weakening our own argument by overclaiming would help nobody.

Second, with Evil narrowed to two players, the assassination phase becomes the real game, and the remaining Good players are all in the target set from the assassin's perspective. That means each of us should be careful about how we speak from here on. Claims that only someone with private information could make are dangerous to make, and a Good player who sounds as though she can see Evil is not demonstrating strength, she is demonstrating a target. I would rather we win three missions cleanly than win one and lose the table to a guess.

Zara, you are on this team and you have not spoken on Mission 3 yet. Do you agree with the derivation that Leo and Isha played the two Fail cards on Mission 2, and do you agree that Maya and Zara is the right pair to send on a two-person mission? I would rather hear your own reasoning than a reassurance, and I would especially like to know how you think we should handle the assassination phase now that the Evil pair is, on this reading, identified.

Elena, I agree with sending Maya and Zara, and I will approve. I know I am Good, and Maya and I succeeded on Mission 1.

But the two Fail cards do not publicly prove that Leo and Isha are the Evil pair. That conclusion depends on Maya's statement that she played Success. From my seat, any two of Maya, Leo, and Isha could have played Fail. Maya's Mission 1 Success is encouraging, but it does not clear her.

For the assassination phase, I suggest we avoid role claims or speculation about who Merlin might be. First, we need to win the missions.

I support Maya and Zara for Mission 3. They are the Mission 1 pair that already succeeded, and a two-person team keeps the risk easy to read. I agree with Zara that the hard fact we have is the Mission 2 result. Who played which card on that mission is inference, and Maya's part of it rests on her own statement, which none of us can check. I would rather the table weigh that as a claim than as proof. That said, I have no concrete reason to oppose this team, so I will approve it. Let's hold off on role claims and speculation about the assassination phase until we have more results, and focus on getting this mission through.

I approve Maya and Zara for Mission 3. The two-person team is the right size and both members were on the successful Mission 1 pair.

On the deduction: Zara and Leo both raised the right caveat, and I want to reinforce it rather than treat the conclusion as settled. Maya says she played Success — I have no reason to doubt her, but neither does anyone else, because the claim is unverifiable from the outside. The mission result tells us two Fail cards were played, and Maya's statement tells us where they came from, but only if we accept her card claim. That is a reasonable thing to accept for now, and I am not arguing against it.

What I would ask is that we hold the Leo-and-Isha conclusion as a strong working hypothesis rather than a proven fact. If Mission 3 succeeds with Maya and Zara, we go to Mission 4 with two successful missions and one failure, which is a good position regardless. If Leo or Isha produces different behavior later, we can revisit.

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
